Paula, November 12. You have five minutes with the team, and the reinsurer is in the room.
Five minutes. Then I need five sentences, one for each part of the story.
Good. Start with the client. Who are they today?
Litoral Cargo is a logistics company in Santos. It has four warehouses and eighty trucks.
And when we started with them, six years ago?
In 2019 the company was small. It had two warehouses, and the first quote was cheap and simple.
Now the fire. The reinsurer always asks about that first.
The team was loading a truck when the fire started. Nobody was using the old machine, and nobody was hurt.

Hi, Paula. David here. Twenty-two years ago I presented a big account alone in Miami for the first time. I was thirty-one, and I was terrified, so I did the worst thing possible: I wrote three pages and I learned them by heart. Word by word. In the room, I said two sentences, and then my head was completely empty. Nothing. I stood there in silence for eleven seconds. Eleven seconds is a very long time when eight people are looking at you. After the meeting, an old broker took me for a coffee, and he was kind but he was honest. He said: nobody in that room wanted a speech. They wanted five things. Who the client is. What the history is. What the loss was. What the numbers say. And what happens next. He wrote them on a paper napkin, five short lines, and he gave it to me. I still do that today, before every presentation. One small card, five sentences, one for each part of the story. And here is why it works, Paula, and this is the only thing I want you to remember: you cannot forget five sentences. And if you lose one of them, the other four are still there, and nobody in the room knows anything was missing. See you soon.

Good morning, Paula. Sofia here. I want to tell you one thing before your lesson today, and then I will leave you alone. In January, in my office, you said one sentence to me. You said: I understand a little, but I cannot speak. I remember it exactly, because I wrote it down. Now listen to this week. On Monday you answered Greg's call in English, at seven in the morning, alone. On Tuesday you read the incident report from the site manager, and you did not ask me for a translation. On Wednesday you compared two quotes and you recommended one, with a reason. On Thursday you called the client and you asked him three questions on the phone. And your report notes are in English now. I have five of them here on my desk. That is one week, Paula. One week. And you did not notice any of it, because it happened slowly, one lesson at a time. Now the practical part. The flight and the hotel for November twelve are booked. You have five minutes with the team, and the reinsurer is in the room. And I want you to hear one thing about that room: it is not a test. Nobody there is waiting for a mistake. They only want to understand the account, and you are the person in this company who knows it best. See you Thursday.
